rv.q: This, Lyndsey Turner’s gripping revival at the National magnificently manages to do.
A great play has found a powerful, timely production.
It's a play of sensory beauty and moral ugliness, showing that no drug is more powerful than self-righteousness, whatever side you're on.
Nevertheless, this is an instructive rather than an alarming evening, an occasion on which it is easier to spot the parallels than be chilled by them.
This is the National firing on all cylinders.
Director Lyndsey Turner makes the three hours of morality flawed – and floored – by madness fly by.
It's another masterly touch in a production that hardly puts a foot wrong.
Turner’s vision of The Crucible is bleak but hugely rewarding, digging deep into the violent paranoia and creating a convincing blood lust dressed up as justice that grips Salem.
Turner's symbolism and exquisite abstraction make this an excellent, faithful transposition of the original material.
In serving Miller’s text with discipline and care, Turner's staging is both sturdy and elegant, allowing contrary impulses to clash with shattering results.

The danger that threatens these people is presented as a continual presence in this production by the appearance in the chiaroscuro shadows far upstage of the child accusers or of things being enacted as they are referred to downstage.
Ironically, this entirely self-conscious production’s attempt to add more weight is what stifles the play.
Turner's direction pushes Miller's dialogue to its absolute zenith. So forceful is the tension, every lie told by the accusers, every plea made by the innocent will have you gripped.
The final reconciliation scene in prison with his wife Elizabeth – an impressive performance from Eileen Walsh – is genuinely moving.
Just a few more moments like that would convince me this is the finest Crucible of modern times. It's still not far off.
The acting is rich and gripping, and the staging gorgeous, but for those wishing for something beyond the aesthetics, I fear this Crucible falls short.

cn.t: Turner's visually spectacular production features arresting design elements like a cascading rain curtain, but critics split on whether the operatic staging enhances or overwhelms Miller's classic drama.

vr.q: an important play a terrific production and impressive performances only marred by a tendency at times towards melodrama
